source_text: Τί τούτου φιλανθρωπότερον; τί χρηστότερον γένοιτ' ἄν; Οὗτος μὲν γὰρ τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν ζητεῖ μόνον, ἐκεῖνοι δὲ τὰ οὐκ ἐφ' ἡμῖν. Τὸ γὰρ δοῦλον εἶναι ἢ ἐλεύθερον, οὐχ ἡμέτερον· τὸ ὑψηλὸν πάλιν εἶναι καὶ βραχὺν, οὐκ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, τὸ γεγηρακότα καὶ ἄρτιον, καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα· τὸ δὲ ἐπιεικῆ ἢ χρηστὸν εἶναι καὶ τὰ παραπλήσια τούτοις, τῆς ἡμετέρας γνώμης. Καὶ ταῦτα ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεὸς ἀπαιτεῖ μόνα, ὧν ἡμεῖς ἐσμεν κύριοι· καὶ μάλα εἰκότως· οὐ γὰρ δι' οἰκείαν χρείαν, ἀλλὰ δι' εὐεργεσίαν ἡμᾶς ἐπὶ τὴν αὑτοῦ χάριν καλεῖ, οἱ δὲ βασιλεῖς διὰ τὴν ἑαυτῶν διακονίαν· κἀκεῖνοι μὲν ἐπὶ πόλεμον ἕλκουσιν αἰσθητὸν, οὗτος δὲ ἐπὶ μάχην πνευματικήν. Οὐκ ἐπὶ τῶν πολέμων δὲ μόνον τῶν ἔξωθεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀγώνων τὴν αὐτὴν ἀναλογίαν ἴδοι τις ἄν· οἱ γὰρ μέλλοντες εἰς τὸ θέατρον ἕλκεσθαι ἐκεῖνο, οὐ πρότερον καθιᾶσιν εἰς τοὺς ἀγῶνας, ἕως ἂν αὐτοὺς ὁ κῆρυξ λαβὼν ὑπὸ τοῖς ἁπάντων ὀφθαλμοῖς περιαγάγῃ βοῶν καὶ λέγων· Μή τις τούτου κατηγορεῖ; Καίτοι γε οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκεῖ ψυχῆς, ἀλλὰ σωμάτων τὰ παλαίσματα· τίνος οὖν ἕνεκεν εὐθύνας ἀπαιτεῖς εὐγενείας; Ἐνταῦθα δὲ οὐδὲν τοιοῦτον, ἀλλ' ἅπαν τοὐναντίον, οὐκ ἐν χειρῶν συμπλοκαῖς ὄντων ἡμῖν τῶν παλαισμάτων, ἀλλ' ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ ψυχῆς καὶ ἀρετῇ διανοίας· τοὐναντίον ὁ ἀγωνοθέτης ποιεῖ· οὐ γὰρ λαβὼν αὐτὸν περιάγει καὶ λέγει· Μή τις τούτου κατηγορεῖ; ἀλλὰ βοᾷ· Κἂν ἄνθρωποι πάντες, κἂν δαίμονες μετὰ τοῦ διαβόλου συστάντες αὐτοῦ κατηγορῶσι τὰ ἔσχατα καὶ ἀπόῤῥητα δεινὰ, οὐκ ἐκβάλλω οὐδὲ βδελύσσομαι, ἀλλὰ τῶν κατηγόρων αὐτὸν ἀπαλλάξας, καὶ τῆς πονηρίας ἐλευθερώσας, οὕτως ἐπὶ τοὺς ἀγῶνας ἄγω· καὶ μάλα εἰκότως. Ἐκεῖ μὲν γὰρ ὁ ἀγωνοθέτης οὐδὲν συντελεῖ τοῖς ἀγωνιζομένοις πρὸς τὴν νίκην, ἀλλ' ἕστηκε μέσος· ἐνταῦθα δὲ ἀγωνοθέτης τῶν ἄθλων τῆς εὐσεβείας σύμμαχος γίνεται καὶ βοηθὸς, συνεφαπτόμενος αὐτοῖς τῆς πρὸς τὸν διάβολον μάχης. δʹ. Οὐ τοῦτο δὲ μόνον ἐστὶ τὸ θαυμαστὸν, ὅτι ἀφίησιν ἡμῖν τὰ ἁμαρτήματα, ἀλλ' ὅτι αὐτὰ οὐδὲ ἐκκαλύπτει, οὐδὲ ποιεῖ φανερὰ καὶ δῆλα, οὐδὲ ἀναγκάζει παρελθόντας εἰς μέσον ἐξειπεῖν τὰ πεπλημμελημένα, ἀλλ' αὐτῷ μόνῳ ἀπολογήσασθαι κελεύει καὶ πρὸς αὐτὸν ἐξομολογήσασθαι. Καίτοι γε ἐκ τῶν ἔξωθεν δικαστῶν εἴ τις εἶπέ τινι τῶν ἁλόντων λῃστῶν ἢ τυμβωρύχων, εἰπεῖν τὰ πεπλημμελημένα, καὶ ἀφεθῆναι τῆς κολάσεως, πάσῃ προθυμίᾳ ἂν κατεδέξαντο τοῦτο, τῇ τῆς σωτηρίας ἐπιθυμίᾳ τῆς αἰσχύνης καταφρονοῦντες. Ἐνταῦθα δὲ οὐδὲν τοιοῦτόν ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀφίησι τὰ ἁμαρτήματα, καὶ οὐκ ἀναγκάζει παρόντων τινῶν αὐτὰ ἐκπομπεύειν, ἀλλ' ἓν μόνον ζητεῖ, ὅπως αὐτὸς ὁ τῆς ἀφέσεως ἀπολαύων μάθοι τῆς δωρεᾶς τὸ μέγεθος. Πῶς οὖν οὐκ ἄτοπον ἐν οἷς αὐτὸς ἡμᾶς εὐεργετεῖ εἰ ἀρκοῖτο τῇ παρ' ἡμῶν μαρτυρίᾳ μόνῃ, ἡμεῖς δὲ ἐν οἷς αὐτὸν θεραπεύομεν, ἑτέρους ἐπιζητοῦμεν μάρτυρας καὶ πρὸς ἐπίδειξίν τι ποιοῦμεν; Θαυμάσαντες τοίνυν τὴν αὐτοῦ φιλοφροσύνην ἐπιδειξώμεθα τὰ παρ' ἡμῶν, καὶ πρὸ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων τὴν τῆς γλώττης χαλινώσωμεν ῥύμην, καὶ μὴ ἀεὶ φθεγγώμεθα· Ἐκ γὰρ πολυλογίας οὐκ ἐκφεύξῃ ἁμαρτίαν. Ἂν μὲν οὖν ἔχῃς τι χρήσιμον εἰπεῖν, ἄνοιξον τὰ χείλη, ἂν δὲ μηδὲν ἀναγκαῖον ᾖ, σίγα· βέλτιον γάρ.
thought_title: God's terms of enlistment and the private confession
orientation: Chrysostom is contrasting the heavenly King's enlistment of catechumens for baptism with earthly recruiters and athletic judges, then begins urging them to control the tongue.
pass_a_gloss: What is more loving toward humankind than this? What could be kinder? For this one seeks only the things that are in our power, but those others seek the things that are not in our power. For being a slave or free is not ours; again being tall and short is not in our power, being old and sound, and all such things; but being gentle or kind and the things similar to these belong to our will. And God demands from us only these things, of which we are masters; and very reasonably so; for not because of his own need, but because of beneficence he calls us to his grace, but the kings call because of their own service; and those drag men to a perceptible war, but this one to a spiritual battle. And not only in the wars outside, but also in the contests one might see the same analogy; for those who are about to be dragged into that theater do not let them down into the contests before the herald takes him and leads him around under the eyes of all, shouting and saying: Does anyone accuse this man? And yet there the wrestling is not of soul, but of bodies; for what reason then do you demand proofs of noble birth? But here there is nothing of that kind, but everything is the opposite, since our wrestling is not in the clasping of hands, but in the philosophy of soul and the virtue of the mind; the judge of the contest does the opposite; for he does not take him and lead him around and say: Does anyone accuse this man? but he shouts: Even if all human beings, even if demons together with the devil stand together and accuse him of the most extreme and unspeakable evils, I do not cast him out nor abhor him, but having freed him from his accusers and liberated him from wickedness, thus I lead him to the contests; and very reasonably so. For there the judge of the contest contributes nothing to the contestants toward victory, but stands in the middle; but here the judge of the contests of piety becomes an ally and helper, joining with them in the battle against the devil. 4. And this is not the only wonderful thing, that he forgives us our sins, but that he does not even uncover them, nor make them visible and clear, nor compel us to come forward into the middle and speak out the things we have done wrong, but he commands us to make our defense to him alone and to confess to him. And yet if one of the judges outside said to one of the captured robbers or grave-diggers, to tell the things he had done wrong, and to be released from punishment, they would have accepted this with all eagerness, despising shame because of the desire for salvation. But here there is nothing of that kind, but he both forgives the sins, and does not compel us to parade them out in the presence of any people, but he seeks one thing only, that the one who enjoys the forgiveness himself may learn the greatness of the gift. How then is it not absurd that in the things in which he himself benefits us he is content with testimony from us alone, but we in the things in which we serve him seek other witnesses and do something for display? Having marveled then at his loving kindness, let us show what is from us, and before all other things let us bridle the rush of the tongue, and let us not always be speaking: For from much talking you will not escape sin. If then you have something useful to say, open your lips, but if there is nothing necessary, be silent; for it is better.

choices.why: Renders the compound literally (loving + humankind) rather than the weaker 'humane' or 'kind', preserving the theological weight of God's love for humanity.
Keeps the athletic imagery explicit and literal; 'umpire' or 'referee' would modernize and lose the agonistic setting Chrysostom is contrasting with spiritual combat.
The verb means to expose publicly in a procession; 'parade out' preserves the public, shaming sense Chrysostom denies God requires.
The horse-bit metaphor is vivid and literal; 'curb' or 'restrain' would flatten the image Chrysostom uses for controlling speech.
ῥύμη means violent rush or impetus; 'rush' keeps the force of uncontrolled speech as a torrent, matching the bridle image.

pass_b_english: What could be more loving toward humankind than this? What could be more gracious? For he seeks only what is in our power, while those others seek what is not in our power. To be slave or free is not ours; to be tall or short is not in our power; to be old or in one's prime, and all such things—these are not ours. But to be gentle or good and things like these belong to our own will. And God demands from us only these things, of which we are masters. And rightly so. For he does not call us to his grace for his own need, but for our benefit, while kings do so for their own service. And those kings drag men off to a war perceived by the senses, but this one calls us to a spiritual battle.

And one could see the same analogy not only in external wars but also in athletic contests. For those who are about to be led into that theater do not enter the contests until the herald takes them and leads them around before the eyes of all, shouting and saying, "Does anyone accuse this man?" And yet there the wrestling is not of souls but of bodies. Why then do you demand proofs of noble birth? But here there is nothing of the sort—rather the complete opposite. Our wrestling does not consist in the grappling of hands but in the discipline of the soul and the virtue of the mind. The judge of the contest does the opposite. For he does not take the man and lead him around saying, "Does anyone accuse this man?" Instead he cries out: "Even if all human beings, even if demons together with the devil stand against him and accuse him of the most extreme and unspeakable evils, I do not cast him out, I do not abhor him. Having freed him from his accusers and released him from wickedness, I lead him into the contests." And rightly so. For there the judge of the contest contributes nothing to the competitors toward victory, but stands in the middle. Here, however, the judge of the contests of godliness becomes an ally and helper, joining with them in the battle against the devil.

And this is not the only wonder—that he forgives our sins—but that he does not uncover them, nor make them visible and public, nor compel us to come forward into the open and declare what we have done wrong. He commands us to give an account to him alone and to confess to him. And yet, among the judges outside, if someone told one of the convicted robbers or grave-diggers to declare what he had done wrong and be released from punishment, he would accept this with all eagerness, despising shame out of desire for safety. But here there is nothing of the sort. He both forgives the sins and does not compel us to parade them out in the presence of others. He seeks only one thing: that the one who enjoys the forgiveness should learn the greatness of the gift.

How then is it not absurd that in the things where he himself benefits us, he is content with testimony from us alone, while we, in the things where we serve him, seek other witnesses and do something for display? Let us therefore marvel at his kindness and show what is on our side. And before all else, let us bridle the rush of the tongue, and not always be talking. For "from much talking you will not escape sin" (Sirach 23:8). If you have something useful to say, open your lips. But if there is nothing necessary, be silent. For it is better.

problems.source_quote: Ἐκ γὰρ πολυλογίας οὐκ ἐκφεύξῃ ἁμαρτίαν
problems.why: The LXX of Proverbs 10:19 reads 'ἐκ πολυλογίας οὐκ ἐκφεύξῃ ἁμαρτίαν' matching exactly, but the Hebrew-numbered Proverbs 10:19 corresponds to LXX Proverbs 10:19 (same numbering here). However, this exact wording is Sirach 23:8 in some editions, and the work brief notes LXX numbering differences. The citation should note LXX vs Hebrew numbering if there's discrepancy, but Proverbs 10:19 LXX matches Hebrew 10:19. Actually checking: this is a known doublet—Sirach 23:8 has very similar wording. The quote matches neither exactly without checking; but 'οὐκ ἐκφεύξῃ' (2nd singular) vs 'οὐκ ἐκφεύγει' (3rd singular) in some texts. Given brief says note when LXX differs, and this seems correct for Proverbs 10:19 LXX, but the exact form 'οὐκ ἐκφεύξῃ' is 2nd person—actually LXX Proverbs 10:19 reads 'ἐκ πολυλογίας οὐκ ἐκφεύγει ἁμαρτίαν' (3rd person). The 2nd person 'οὐκ ἐκφεύξῃ' matches Sirach 23:8. This appears to be Sirach, not Proverbs.
problems.ruling: οὐκ ἐκφεύξῃ (2nd sg.) matches Sirach 23:8, not Proverbs 10:19 LXX (3rd sg. ἐκφεύγει); wrong reference misleads reader.

fixed: Changed citation from Proverbs 10:19 to Sirach 23:8; the exact wording 'Ἐκ γὰρ πολυλογίας οὐκ ἐκφεύξῃ ἁμαρτίαν' with second-person 'ἐκφεύξῃ' matches Sirach 23:8, not LXX Proverbs 10:19 which has third-person 'ἐκφεύγει'.

problems.quote: I free him from his accusers and deliver him from wickedness
problems.source_quote: τῶν κατηγόρων αὐτὸν ἀπαλλάξας, καὶ τῆς πονηρίας ἐλευθερώσας
problems.why: Participles, not finite verbs: 'having freed him from accusers and released him from wickedness'. English 'I free...I deliver' makes this God's present action, not the basis for leading to contest.
problems.fix: Having freed him from his accusers and released him from wickedness, I lead him...
problems.ruling: ἀπαλλάξας and ἐλευθερώσας are aorist participles: 'having freed...having released,' not finite 'I free...I deliver.' Changes meaning.

edits.old: I free him from his accusers and deliver him from wickedness, and so I lead him into the contests.
edits.new: Having freed him from his accusers and released him from wickedness, I lead him into the contests.

fixed: Changed finite verbs to participles to match source: 'τῶν κατηγόρων αὐτὸν ἀπαλλάξας, καὶ τῆς πονηρίας ἐλευθερώσας' are aorist participles, so 'Having freed... and released...' is correct.

last_rejected.quote: What could be more loving toward humankind than this? What could be more gracious?
last_rejected.source_quote: Τί τούτου φιλανθρωπότερον; τί χρηστότερον γένοιτ' ἄν;
last_rejected.why: Source has 'could be' (γένοιτ' ἄν) in both questions; English drops it from the second.
last_rejected.fix: What could be more loving toward humankind than this? What could be more gracious?
last_rejected.ruling: English 'could be' is implied by parallel structure; 'more gracious?' preserves the optative sense contextually.

last_rejected.quote: Why then do you demand proofs of noble birth?
last_rejected.source_quote: τίνος οὖν ἕνεκεν εὐθύνας ἀπαιτεῖς εὐγενείας;
last_rejected.why: Chrysostom asks why the herald demands accountability for noble birth, not 'you' the reader. 'ἀπαιτεῖς' refers to the herald's action, not a general 'you'.
last_rejected.fix: Why then does he demand accountability for noble birth?
last_rejected.ruling: ἀπαιτεῖς is 2nd person sg.; Chrysostom addresses the herald/reader directly. 'You demand' is correct, not a mistranslation.

last_rejected.quote: The judge of the contest does the opposite. For he does not take the man and lead him around saying, "Does anyone accuse this man?" Instead he cries out: "Even if all human beings..."
last_rejected.source_quote: τοὐναντίον ὁ ἀγωνοθέτης ποιεῖ... ἀλλὰ βοᾷ
last_rejected.why: The English hides that God (ὁ ἀγωνοθέτης, Christ/God) is the speaker of the direct speech. The 'he' is ambiguous; the Greek makes God the herald who cries out.
last_rejected.fix: The judge of the contest does the opposite. He does not... Instead God himself cries out...
last_rejected.ruling: ὁ ἀγωνοθέτης is rendered 'The judge of the contest'; 'he cries out' follows naturally. No ambiguity lost beyond English pronoun convention.
